name: Chenin Blanc

lines.s10: Chenin Blanc is the Loire's shape shifter: dry, sweet or sparkling, with quince, baked apple and bright acidity in every style.
lines.s20: Chenin Blanc is the white grape of Vouvray and Savennières in the Loire, and of South Africa's old vines. It tastes of quince, yellow apple and honey, and its high acidity carries it from bone dry to richly sweet.
lines.s45: Chenin Blanc does everything a white grape can do, from bone dry to sparkling to honey sweet. Its home is the middle Loire, in Vouvray, Savennières and Anjou. It tastes of quince, yellow apple and honey, with a note like beeswax, and its high acidity keeps even the sweet ones fresh. The Loire mostly keeps new oak away, while South Africa makes riper wines, often from old vines and in barrel. Pour a dry one with roast pork, and an off dry one with spiced food. At the Cape it was long called Steen, and only in the 1960s was it shown to be the Loire's grape.
lines.sale: Chenin Blanc gives you richness and freshness in the same glass: quince and honey on a spine of bright acidity. I would pour a dry Vouvray with the roast pork, or an off dry one with anything spiced.

glass.lead: Quince, yellow apple and honey with a waxy, wet wool note, held taut by high acidity at any sweetness.

ladder.where: Vouvray, Montlouis and Savennières in the middle Loire
Swartland, Stellenbosch and Paarl in South Africa

glass.structure: Dry to lusciously sweet. Acidity high at every sweetness, alcohol moderate, body medium; fuller in ripe, barrel raised South African wines.

old.where: The middle Loire: Vouvray, Montlouis, Savennières, Anjou and the Layon
old.glass: Tends to be taut and chalky: quince, yellow apple and lemon with chamomile, beeswax and a wet wool note, at moderate alcohol. It may be dry, off dry or sweet, and the acidity is high throughout.
old.cellar: Usually fermented in steel or old casks, with little new oak; the year decides whether a wine is dry, off dry, sweet or sparkling.

new.where: South Africa: Swartland, Stellenbosch, Paarl and the wider Western Cape
new.glass: Typically riper and broader: yellow apple, ripe pear, pineapple and guava, often with honeyed melon and a fuller body. Everyday bottles are fresh and fruity; old vine wines are richer, with vanilla and toasted almond from barrels.
new.cellar: Two broad styles: unwooded wines made cold in steel for early drinking, and richer old bush vine wines, often fermented and aged in barrel.

contrast.why: The Cape is warmer and sunnier than the Loire, so the fruit ripens further and alcohol rises; old, low yielding bush vines add concentration. The Loire names a place and a sweetness, South Africa the grape.
contrast.blur: Savennières and warm Loire years can be rich and powerful, some Loire growers now use barrels, and cooler Cape sites make lean, taut, unwooded wines.
contrast.call: Chalk, wet wool and piercing acidity at moderate alcohol lean Loire; riper pineapple and guava, more body and often vanilla from barrels lean South Africa.

service.temp: 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius; rich barrel aged wines a little warmer, sweet ones colder.
service.glass: A white wine glass; a small glass for the sweet wines and a tulip for the sparkling.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary; a young, tight Savennières can open with a short decant.
service.age: Most dry wines within five years, Savennières ten or more; sweet Vouvray and Layon wines keep for decades.

with.why: quince and apple in the wine meet the pork

with.dish: Roast chicken or veal in cream
with.why: acidity cuts the cream, body matches the dish
an off dry wine cools the cayenne
for the sweet wines: honey against caramel or salt

labels.means: Chenin Blanc from Touraine in the Loire: dry, off dry, sweet or sparkling, so read the label.
Dry, off dry and sweet: the sweetness words on a Loire Chenin Blanc.
A dry, firm, long lived Chenin Blanc from Anjou, on the Loire near Angers.
Sweet Chenin Blanc from Anjou, often touched by noble rot; Bonnezeaux and Quarts de Chaume lie within it.
The old South African name for Chenin Blanc, still seen on some labels.

guest.a: Either. Vouvray is Chenin Blanc, and it comes dry, off dry, sweet and sparkling. Look for sec for dry, demi-sec for a touch of sweetness and moelleux for sweet.

guest.q: I usually drink Chardonnay. Would I like this?
guest.a: A dry, barrel raised South African Chenin Blanc is the nearest thing: full and round, with ripe pear and a little vanilla. It has brighter acidity than most Chardonnay.

guest.q: What is that waxy, woolly smell?
guest.a: It is the grape's own mark, often described as beeswax, lanolin or wet wool. Tasters look for it beside quince and honey to recognise Chenin Blanc.

compare.tell: Riesling shows lime, white peach and, with age, petrol; Chenin Blanc shows quince, baked apple and wet wool on a broader body.
Chardonnay is rounder, with lower acidity and no waxy, woolly note; Chenin Blanc keeps a sharper edge and tastes of quince and honey.
Sémillon is waxy too, but softer in acidity, with lemon and toast as it ages; Chenin Blanc is sharper, with quince and apple.

cards.front: Chenin Blanc: name its Loire homes and its old South African name.
cards.back: Vouvray, Montlouis, Savennières and Anjou in the middle Loire. In South Africa it was long called Steen, and was matched to the Loire's grape in the 1960s.

cards.front: Chenin Blanc blind: Loire or South Africa, what tips it?
cards.back: Chalk, wet wool and piercing acidity at moderate alcohol lean Loire. Riper pineapple and guava, more body and often vanilla from barrels lean South Africa.

cards.front: On a Vouvray, which is Chenin Blanc, what do sec, demi-sec and moelleux mean?
cards.back: The sweetness. Sec is dry, demi-sec is off dry and moelleux is sweet. Vouvray is also made sparkling, as pétillant or mousseux.

questions.q: Two dry Chenin Blancs are poured blind. One is taut, with quince, chalk and a wet wool note at moderate alcohol; the other is fuller, with pineapple, guava and vanilla. Which pair of origins fits, in that order?
questions.exp: Chalk, wet wool and piercing acidity at moderate alcohol tend to mark the Loire. Riper pineapple and guava, a fuller body and vanilla from barrels tend to mark South Africa's old vine wines.

questions.q: A guest wants a Vouvray with only a touch of sweetness for a spiced pork dish. Which word on the label do you look for?
questions.exp: Demi-sec is off dry: a touch of sweetness balanced by high acidity. Sec is dry, moelleux is fully sweet, and brut is the word for a dry sparkling wine.

questions.q: A blind white is medium gold and off dry, with quince, baked apple, honey and a wet wool note over searing acidity. Which grape is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: Honeyed quince and baked apple with wet wool over searing acidity is Chenin Blanc. Riesling would show lime and often petrol, and Chardonnay and Sémillon have softer acidity.

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it, though TASTE.world reads old: the Loire stands against South Africa, which the reviewed profile already names.
Steen is said to have been matched to Chenin Blanc in the 1960s with no year: the South African bodies give 1963 and a standard reference work gives 1965.
Left out: the claim that a document of 845 names the grape as Plant d'Anjou. One trade body states it and the reference works doubt it.
Lanolin sits in the honeyed group beside beeswax, and wet wool is named in the prose, for want of a waxy family among the nineteen.
The Court's grid calls Vouvray cool and TASTE.clim says moderate; the ladder follows the grid and gives the Loire the cool rung.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
